savoury = having a salty or spicy flavour rather than a sweet one
bland = with very little flavour
stale = no longer fresh, especially bread or biscuits
perishable = likely to go bad quickly if not kept cold
pungent = having a very strong smell or taste
tangy = having a sharp, pleasant taste, often of citrus or yoghurt
succulent = tender and full of juice
palatable = pleasant enough to eat or drink
unpalatable = unpleasant to eat; hard to accept
mouth-watering = looking or smelling so good that you want to eat it
appetising = making you want to eat because of how it looks or smells
rancid = smelling or tasting unpleasant because fat has gone bad
soggy = unpleasantly wet and soft
crunchy = firm and making a sharp sound when you bite
tender = soft and easy to cut or chew
tough = difficult to chew because the meat is hard
lean meat = meat with little fat
wholesome = good for your health; made from simple, decent ingredients
nutritious = containing substances the body needs to stay healthy
moreish = so pleasant that you want another mouthful
sickly-sweet = too sweet in an unpleasant way
piping hot = very hot, especially of food just served
tepid = only slightly warm, often when it should be hotter
seasoning = salt, pepper or spices added to improve flavour
garnish = a small amount of food used to decorate a dish
condiment = a sauce or seasoning eaten with food, such as mustard
marinade = a flavoured liquid in which you soak food before cooking
pulses = dried seeds such as beans, lentils and peas used as food
staple food = a basic food that a population eats regularly
wholegrain = made from the complete grain, not only the refined part
saturated fat = a type of fat, often from animals, that should be eaten in limited amounts
dietary fibre = the part of plants that helps digestion and is not fully absorbed
additive = a substance added to food to colour, preserve or flavour it
preservative = a substance added so that food lasts longer
flavour enhancer = a substance added to make food taste stronger
gluten = a protein in wheat and some other grains that some people cannot eat
lactose = the natural sugar found in milk
fortified = having extra vitamins or minerals added
skimmed milk = milk from which almost all the fat has been removed
full-fat = containing all the natural fat, not reduced
gone off = no longer safe or pleasant to eat because it is too old
use-by date = the last date a perishable food should be eaten for safety
best-before date = the date until which a food is at its best quality
shelf life = how long a food stays good to eat under proper storage
food poisoning = an illness caused by eating contaminated food
contamination = the presence of harmful bacteria or substances in food
cross-contamination = the spread of harmful bacteria from one food or surface to another
simmer = to cook just below boiling point, with small bubbles
roast = to cook food in an oven with fat, often meat or vegetables
ferment = to change food through the action of yeast or bacteria
sauté = to fry quickly in a small amount of fat
stew = to cook slowly in liquid; a dish cooked that way
braise = to fry food briefly and then cook it slowly in a little liquid
poach = to cook gently in water or another liquid that is not quite boiling
blanch = to put food briefly into boiling water, then often into cold water
pickle = to preserve food in vinegar or salt water
cure = to preserve meat or fish with salt, smoke or both
marinate = to leave food in a flavoured liquid so it absorbs taste
knead = to press and fold dough with your hands
whisk = to beat eggs or cream quickly until light
fold in = to mix a light ingredient into a heavier one with gentle movements
carve = to cut cooked meat into slices for serving
mince = to cut or grind meat into very small pieces
drizzle = to pour a thin stream of liquid over food
stir-fry = to cook small pieces of food quickly in a little oil while stirring
deep-fry = to cook food by covering it in hot oil
casserole = a dish of meat or vegetables cooked slowly in liquid in the oven
stock = a flavoured liquid made by cooking bones, meat or vegetables in water
gravy = a sauce made from meat juices, often served with a roast
batter = a mixture of flour, egg and liquid used to coat food or make pancakes
dough = a thick mixture of flour and liquid that is baked
yeast = a microscopic fungus used to make bread rise
sourdough = bread made with a fermented starter rather than commercial yeast
prove = to leave dough in a warm place so that it rises before baking
glaze = to brush food with egg, sugar or jelly so it shines
caramelise = to heat sugar or vegetables until they brown and sweeten
reduce = to boil a liquid so that some water evaporates and the flavour strengthens
thicken = to make a sauce or soup less watery
infuse = to leave a flavouring in a liquid so the taste passes into it
balanced diet = a way of eating that includes a healthy mix of food groups
vegan = eating no animal products, including milk, eggs and honey
pescatarian = a person who does not eat meat but does eat fish
flexitarian = a person who mainly eats plant food but occasionally eats meat
intolerance = difficulty digesting a food, causing discomfort but not a full allergy
nutrient = a substance in food that the body needs, such as a vitamin or protein
malnutrition = poor health caused by not having enough of the right foods
undernourished = not getting enough food or nutrients to stay healthy
obesity = the state of having so much body fat that it harms health
calorie intake = the amount of energy you get from food and drink
empty calories = energy from food that offers little nutritional value
crash diet = a very strict, short-term eating plan that cuts food severely
fad diet = a fashionable eating plan that promises fast results with little evidence
yo-yo dieting = repeatedly losing weight and then gaining it again
portion control = choosing sensible amounts of food rather than eating until the plate is empty
fasting = going without food for a set time, often for health or religion
intermittent fasting = an eating pattern with regular periods of not eating
supplement = a pill or powder taken to add nutrients to your diet
antioxidant = a substance in some foods thought to protect cells from damage
probiotic = a food or drink containing live bacteria that may help the gut
fluid intake = the amount of liquid you drink
dehydrated = lacking enough water in the body
plant-based = made mainly or entirely from plants rather than animals
dairy-free = containing no milk or products made from milk
high-protein = containing a large amount of protein
low-carb = containing little starch or sugar
sugar-free = containing no added sugar
wholefood = food that is as close as possible to its natural state
eating disorder = a serious mental health condition involving harmful eating patterns
binge = an episode of eating a very large amount of food in a short time
comfort food = food you eat because it makes you feel emotionally better
emotional eating = eating in response to feelings rather than hunger
foodie = a person who is very interested in cooking and trying dishes
gourmet = connected with high-quality, carefully prepared food
nutritionist = a person who advises on food and nutrients, not always a regulated doctor
dietitian = a qualified health professional who gives evidence-based diet advice
fussy eater = a person who refuses many foods and accepts only a few
tip = extra money left for waiting staff for their service
reservation = an arrangement to have a table kept for you at a set time
Michelin star = a mark of excellence given to a restaurant by the Michelin guide
à la carte = ordered as individual dishes from a menu, not as a fixed set
set menu = a limited list of dishes offered at a fixed price
tasting menu = a sequence of small dishes chosen by the chef
sommelier = a restaurant specialist who advises on wine
service charge = an extra percentage added to a restaurant bill for staff
cover charge = a fixed fee some restaurants add per person before food
table manners = the polite way of eating and behaving during a meal
aperitif = a drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite
mocktail = a mixed drink without alcohol
fully booked = having no free tables left
walk-in = a customer who arrives without a reservation
fine dining = formal, high-quality restaurant food and service
street food = ready-to-eat food sold from stalls or carts
food truck = a vehicle from which cooked food is sold
sharing platter = a large plate of food designed for several people to share
overpriced = costing more than it is worth
value for money = worth the price you pay because of quality or quantity
food critic = a journalist who reviews restaurants and dishes
signature dish = the recipe a cook or restaurant is best known for
chef's special = a dish recommended or created by the chef that day
dietary requirement = a need to avoid or include certain foods for health or belief
allergen = a substance that can cause an allergic reaction
halal = prepared according to Islamic rules, especially of meat
kosher = prepared according to Jewish dietary law
corkage = a fee for bringing your own wine into a restaurant
house wine = the restaurant's ordinary, usually cheaper wine
processed food = food that has been changed from its natural state, often with additives
food waste = edible food that is thrown away instead of being eaten
organic = produced without synthetic pesticides or fertilisers
fair trade = a system that aims to pay producers in poorer countries a fairer price
food security = reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
food miles = the distance food travels from where it is produced to where it is eaten
factory farming = keeping large numbers of animals in intensive conditions for cheap meat or eggs
farm-to-table = food served soon after it is grown, with few middlemen
battery farming = keeping hens in small cages to produce eggs cheaply
free-range = allowed to move outdoors, especially of hens or their eggs
animal welfare = the health and living conditions of animals kept by humans
livestock = farm animals such as cattle, sheep and pigs
genetically modified = having genes changed in a laboratory to give a plant or animal new traits
food additive = a substance put in food to colour, preserve or flavour it
superfood = a food marketed as especially rich in nutrients
sustainable farming = growing food in a way that can continue without ruining soil, water or wildlife
sustainable seafood = fish caught or farmed in a way that does not empty the oceans
seasonal produce = fruit and vegetables harvested at the natural time of year
locally sourced = obtained from nearby farms or producers
food labelling = the information printed on packaging about ingredients and nutrition
traceability = the ability to follow a food back to where it was produced
supply chain = the sequence of steps that takes food from farm to shop
supermarket chain = a company that owns many large food shops
food shortage = a situation in which there is not enough food available
food desert = a neighbourhood with few shops selling fresh, healthy food
food bank = a charity that gives donated food to people who cannot afford it
food poverty = not being able to afford enough healthy food
ultra-processed = made mostly from industrial ingredients rather than whole foods
convenience food = food that is quick to prepare, often packaged or ready-made
ready meal = a complete dish sold cooked, which you only need to heat
trans fat = an industrial fat, now widely restricted, that harms heart health
cholesterol = a fatty substance in blood; some foods can affect its level
sugar tax = a government charge on drinks with a lot of added sugar
compostable packaging = wrapping that can break down into soil in a compost bin
artificial sweetener = a chemical used instead of sugar to make food taste sweet
